Numbness or tingling over the top of the shoulder usually means the straps are compressing nerves and the load has migrated off the hips; hip-belt chafing over the crest is a friction problem answered by a smoother base layer rather than a tighter belt.

sections.heading: Footwear, Socks and the Interface With the Ground
sections.body: Every force between you and the earth passes through a few square centimetres of sole and a layer of fabric, and problems there disable walkers more often than fitness does. Fit is the whole game and it is routinely got wrong. Leave roughly a centimetre, about a thumb's width, between the longest toe and the front of the shoe, because on a descent the foot slides forward and a toe that touches the end will bruise and eventually lose its nail. Feet also swell during a long day and over consecutive days, commonly by up to half a size, so fit shoes at the end of the day, wearing the socks you will actually walk in, and buy for the larger foot, since most people have one. The heel must be held with minimal lift, since a heel moving up and down inside the shoe is the classic mechanism for a heel blister. Width matters as much as length; a forefoot squeezed narrow causes metatarsal pain and numbness between the toes. Choosing between a stiff boot and a flexible shoe is a genuine trade-off rather than a matter of fashion. A stiffer sole and higher cuff give better protection on sharp talus, better edging on hard ground, and support under a heavy pack, at the cost of weight and reduced ground feel. A lighter shoe reduces the expensive mass at the end of the swinging leg, dries faster and allows more natural foot movement, but transmits more of the ground and offers less protection. The evidence that high cuffs prevent ankle sprains is weaker than folk wisdom suggests. Waterproof membranes keep out light wet but hold water in once flooded and dry very slowly, which is why many walkers in warm wet conditions deliberately choose non-waterproof shoes. Lacing is an adjustable tool. Loosen the forefoot and tighten the ankle for descents; use a heel-lock, in which the lace passes through the top eyelets to form loops on each side and crosses through them, to stop heel lift without crushing the instep. Skip a painful eyelet by running the lace straight up that segment. Socks are the friction interface. A well-fitting wool or synthetic sock manages moisture far better than cotton, which holds water, loses loft and macerates skin. Many walkers use a thin liner sock under a thicker one so that the two layers slide against each other rather than the sock sliding against skin, which displaces the shear from the foot to the fabric. Change socks at lunch, dry the pair you removed on the outside of the pack, and treat consistently wet feet as an urgent problem rather than an inconvenience.

sections.heading: Pacing, Breathing and Fuelling Across a Whole Day
sections.body: Technique fails when the physiological envelope is exceeded, so the last component of efficient walking is the management of effort, fluid and food over many hours. The sustainable pace is bounded by your aerobic threshold, below which fat and carbohydrate are burned aerobically and lactate is cleared as fast as it is produced. Above it, effort can be maintained for tens of minutes rather than hours. The practical field measure is the talk test: at a genuinely sustainable pace you can speak a full sentence without gasping. If you can only manage a few words, you are above threshold and borrowing against later. Start the day deliberately slower than feels natural for the first fifteen or twenty minutes; muscle blood flow, joint fluid and breathing all need that long to settle, and a hard start is paid for all day. Plan in time rather than distance. Naismith's rule, one hour per five kilometres plus one hour per 600 metres of ascent, is a reasonable base for a fit walker on good ground with a light pack, and it needs adjusting. Add substantially for a heavy pack, rough or trackless terrain, snow, poor visibility, heat or a large group, since a group moves at the pace of its slowest member minus the cost of regrouping. Langmuir's correction is useful for descent: subtract about ten minutes per 300 metres of descent on gentle slopes, but add ten minutes per 300 metres where the descent is steep, because steep downhill is slow. Fluid needs vary enormously, from perhaps 400 millilitres per hour in cool conditions to more than a litre in heat, and thirst is a reasonable guide for most people on most days. Two errors are worth avoiding at the extremes: arriving at a long dry stretch already behind, and systematically over-drinking plain water on a very long hot effort, which can dilute blood sodium and cause exercise-associated hyponatraemia, a condition that has killed endurance athletes and whose early symptoms of headache, nausea and confusion mimic dehydration. On efforts beyond about four hours in heat, take sodium with fluid, whether from electrolyte mix or salty food. Fuel before you are hungry. Carbohydrate stores can supply roughly ninety minutes to two hours of hard work, and while walking is mostly fat-fuelled, running the tank down produces a disproportionate collapse in pace and judgement. Eating something modest every hour or so from the start is markedly more effective than a single large lunch, and it also avoids the sluggishness that follows one. Rest breaks should be short and frequent rather than long and rare. Five minutes every hour keeps the legs warm, avoids the stiffness that follows a long sit, and costs less total time than the two half-hour halts most groups drift into. Take one longer break mid-day if the weather allows, and use it for feet, water and food. Finally, set the turnaround as a clock time before you start. A party that has agreed to turn back at two o'clock regardless of how close the summit looks decides calmly; a party deciding in the moment, tired and invested, almost always continues.

sections.heading: Hot Spots and Blisters: Prevention and Field Treatment
sections.body: A blister is not a burn or a rub in the everyday sense. It forms when repeated shear force, the skin surface being dragged sideways relative to the tissue beneath, separates layers within the epidermis at the level of the stratum spinosum. The gap fills with fluid drawn from surrounding tissue. Three factors drive it: friction between sock and skin, pressure concentrating that friction on a small area, and moisture, because damp skin has a substantially higher coefficient of friction than dry or thoroughly wet skin. Heat accelerates all three. The warning is the hot spot: a localised patch of burning or stinging before any blister has formed. Acting on it takes about two minutes and reliably prevents the injury. Ignoring it for another hour usually does not. This is the single highest-value habit in this whole subject, and the commonest failure is social, in a group where nobody wants to be the one to call a halt. Say something. Prevention is layered: shoes that fit, socks that manage moisture, a liner sock so the two fabric layers shear against each other, taping known problem areas before they hurt, keeping feet as dry as circumstances allow, and removing grit promptly since a single embedded stone concentrates pressure enormously. Toenails should be cut short and straight before a trip. Deroofing a blister, meaning removing the skin over it, should be avoided in the field. The roof is a sterile biological dressing, and without it you have an open wound on a foot that must keep walking, in a dirty environment, with a real infection risk.
ingredients: Adhesive tape that stays stuck when damp: zinc oxide, kinesiology or good cloth tape, 25 to 38 millimetres wide.
Hydrocolloid blister dressings from any pharmacy, which cushion and keep the area moist while it heals.
Felt or moleskin sheet, cut into a doughnut so the felt takes pressure off the blister instead of pressing on it.
Small scissors, sterile needles or a safety pin, and a lighter or alcohol wipe to sterilise them.
Antiseptic, a few plain adhesive dressings, a skin tincture such as benzoin to improve tape adhesion on sweaty feet, and a bandana for drying.
steps: Stop the moment you feel a hot spot rather than finishing the climb first, and take the shoe and sock off in good light.
Dry the skin, clear grit from shoe and sock, and identify exactly what is rubbing, such as a seam, a fold or a lifting heel.
If the skin is intact, tape smoothly with rounded corners and no wrinkles, extending well beyond the sore area.
If a small blister has formed and is not under walking pressure, leave it intact and cover it with a hydrocolloid dressing.
If it is large or must be loaded, sterilise a needle, pierce the lower edge, press the fluid out gently and leave the roof in place.
Cover it with hydrocolloid, or surround it with a felt doughnut, then tape over the whole arrangement.
Fix the cause before walking on, then watch for spreading redness, pus or fever, which mean infection and an end to the trip.

sections.heading: Overuse Injuries and What Each One Is Telling You
sections.body: Trail injuries divide into the sudden and the accumulated, and the accumulated ones are both far commoner and far more preventable, because each has a recognisable warning phase and a specific technical cause. Anterior knee pain, felt around or behind the kneecap and always worse on descent, is usually patellofemoral pain: the kneecap tracking poorly in its groove under heavy repeated load. Overstriding downhill, weak hip abductors letting the knee fall inward, and a heavy pack all contribute. The technical fixes are shorter steps, softer knees, poles, and hip strengthening between trips. Iliotibial band syndrome presents as sharp lateral knee pain arising abruptly, again typically on descent, after which walking downhill becomes almost impossible while flat walking is tolerable. It is associated with long descents, sidehilling and running shoes worn beyond their life. Medial tibial stress syndrome, commonly called shin splints, produces aching along the inner border of the shin and often follows a rapid increase in load or a lot of hard descent. Persistent focal bone pain that hurts at rest or at night should be taken seriously as a possible stress fracture, which is a reason to stop rather than to push. Achilles tendinopathy shows as stiffness and pain at the back of the heel, worst in the first steps of the morning. Steep sustained ascent, a sudden change in heel height between footwear, and cold starts without any warm-up are typical precipitants. Plantar fasciitis is sharp heel pain on the first steps after rest, easing as you move and returning worse later. Metatarsalgia, burning under the ball of the foot, usually reflects too-narrow footwear or a pack too heavy for the sole's cushioning. The general principles are the same for all of them. Address the technical cause rather than only the symptom, and distinguish soreness, which is diffuse, symmetrical and improves with movement, from injury, which is focal, one-sided, and worsens as you continue. Sharp pain that alters your gait is a signal to stop, because walking differently to protect one structure reliably damages another. Anti-inflammatory drugs can mask a warning you need, and taking them to keep walking on an injury is how a manageable problem becomes a serious one. A sensible loading progression matters more than any single remedy. A widely used guideline is to increase weekly distance, pack weight or total ascent by no more than about ten percent at a time, changing only one variable in a given week. Most trail overuse injuries trace back to a step change: the first big descent of the season, a pack ten kilograms heavier than any previous trip, or new footwear introduced on a long day. Between trips, the highest-return preparation is not more walking but targeted strength. Hip abductor and gluteal work protects the knee by controlling how far it travels inward under load, and slow single-leg calf raises build the Achilles capacity that descent demands. Two chronic complaints are worth naming because they alarm people unnecessarily: burning between the third and fourth toes is often a Morton's neuroma irritated by narrow footwear, and puffy hands after several hours are usually harmless dependent oedema.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong: Fatigue, Cramp, Darkness and Getting Out
sections.body: Efficiency exists to protect a reserve, and the point of the reserve is the day when something goes wrong. What follows is what deterioration looks like and what to do about it. Deep fatigue announces itself in judgement before it appears in the legs. The recognisable signs are stumbling on ground you would have walked cleanly in the morning, taking the same photograph twice, arguing about the map, ceasing to eat or drink because it seems like too much effort, and a creeping conviction that stopping to sort out a problem is not worth the time. Treat any two of these together as a formal signal to stop for ten minutes, eat something, drink, and reassess the plan rather than the pace. Muscle cramp on the trail is common and its cause is contested. The older explanation of dehydration and electrolyte depletion has weak support in the research, and the better-supported model is altered neuromuscular control in a fatigued muscle, where the reflex that normally inhibits contraction is suppressed. Practically, the immediate treatment is passive stretching of the cramping muscle and gentle contraction of its opposite, which works within seconds. Strongly flavoured substances such as pickle juice appear to relieve cramp faster than any absorption could explain, apparently through a reflex triggered in the mouth and throat. Reducing pace and taking salt and carbohydrate is sensible regardless, and repeated cramping is a message that the day is too ambitious. If you are caught out by darkness, slow down substantially and accept that your speed may halve. Wear a headlamp low, on the chest or in the hand rather than on the forehead, because a light beside your eye flattens the ground and erases every shadow, while a light held low casts side shadows that reveal texture and depth. Shorten steps further, use poles, and navigate by deliberate leapfrogging between identified features rather than by momentum. For a genuine injury, the first decisions are the important ones. Stop and assess in a sheltered spot before attempting anything. Put on warm layers immediately, because a stationary casualty cools fast even in mild conditions. Establish where you are precisely enough to describe it. Decide honestly whether the party can self-evacuate at the speed of the injured member, remembering that a supported walk-out takes far longer than the same terrain took inbound and that a wrong self-rescue attempt in poor weather is more dangerous than a comfortable wait. If you call for help, do it early rather than at last light, and stay put once you have given a location. The habits that make all of this survivable are formed on ordinary days. Carry a light insulating layer and a windproof even on a fine forecast, because the difference between an uncomfortable wait and a dangerous one is usually a jacket. Leave your route and expected return time with someone, and make it specific enough to be searched. And practise the small skills, taping a foot, adjusting a pack, walking a scree slope, when nothing is wrong, because you will not learn them well on the day you need them.

guides.safetyNote: Descent, not ascent, causes most trail injuries, and fatigue degrades foot placement and judgement long before it exhausts the legs, so treat the last hour of a day as the most demanding. Sharp pain that changes how you walk means stop, not push on; painkillers taken to keep going mask a warning you need. On snow slopes hard enough that a slip would not stop naturally, walking technique alone is not enough and an ice axe with trained self-arrest is required. In heat over long efforts take sodium with fluid rather than plain water alone, since exercise-associated hyponatraemia from overdrinking can be fatal and its early symptoms resemble dehydration. If someone is injured, insulate them immediately, fix your position precisely, and call for help early rather than at dusk.

guides.title: The Rest Step for Sustained Climbing
guides.summary: How the mountaineer's rest step works, why a locked skeleton lets muscle recover mid-stride, and how to perform, pace, adapt and troubleshoot it across snow, scree, steep ground and altitude on a long ascent.

sections.heading: What the Rest Step Is and Why It Exists
sections.body: The rest step is a way of walking uphill in which the climber deliberately inserts a brief, complete pause into every single stride, standing with one leg locked straight so that body weight is carried by bone rather than by working muscle. The pause may last a quarter of a second on a gentle trail near sea level, or five full seconds and three breaths at 8,000 metres. Its purpose is not to go slowly. Its purpose is to allow the muscles of the supporting leg to switch off entirely, for a moment, on every step, so that blood can flow through them, oxygen can arrive, and metabolic waste can be flushed away before the next contraction begins. Over ten thousand steps in a day this converts a continuous grinding effort into a long series of short efforts separated by genuine micro-recoveries. The difference in what a body can sustain is not marginal. A climber walking normally up a steep slope at altitude will typically be forced to stop, bent over hands on knees, every few minutes; the same climber using a disciplined rest step can often move for an hour or more without a full halt, arriving less depleted. Ordinary walking on flat ground is remarkably economical because it works like an inverted pendulum: the body vaults over a nearly straight supporting leg, exchanging potential and kinetic energy back and forth so that only about 25 percent of the energy has to be supplied fresh by muscle each step. Walking uphill destroys that exchange. Every step must lift the entire body mass, plus a pack, through the vertical rise of the step, and there is no downhill phase to give any of that energy back. The metabolic cost of moving a kilogram of body plus load through one metre of vertical gain is roughly ten to twelve times the cost of moving it a metre horizontally on the flat, and the leg extensors are working near-continuously against gravity for the whole climb. The rest step is the traditional mountaineer's answer to that continuous demand. It is one of a very small handful of techniques that experienced climbers agree makes a genuine, measurable difference to how far and how high an ordinary person can go, and unlike ropework or crampon technique it costs nothing, requires no equipment, is legal and safe anywhere, and can be learned on a staircase. It also transfers directly to hillwalking, backpacking with a heavy load, working on stairs and ladders, and carrying anything heavy up a long slope. The technique's value rises steeply with three variables: the angle of the ground, the weight on your back, and the altitude.

sections.heading: The Physiological Problem: Muscle Perfusion and the Occlusion Threshold
sections.body: The reason a pause helps at all sits in an inconvenient fact about how muscle is supplied with blood. A contracting muscle squeezes the very vessels that feed it. Blood reaches muscle fibres through arterioles and capillaries running between and among them, and when the fibres shorten and thicken they raise the pressure inside the muscle compartment. Once that intramuscular pressure exceeds the pressure in the small arteries supplying the tissue, flow stops. Laboratory measurements consistently place the onset of this impairment somewhere around 20 to 30 percent of a maximal voluntary contraction, with flow essentially fully occluded by somewhere between 50 and 70 percent depending on the muscle, the joint angle and the individual. The exact figures vary between studies and between muscle groups, so treat any single number with caution, but the shape of the relationship is not in doubt: a muscle held under moderate to hard sustained tension is starving itself. This produces a vicious sequence. Deprived of oxygen delivery, the muscle must generate adenosine triphosphate anaerobically through glycolysis, which is fast but yields only about two molecules of ATP per glucose against roughly thirty when oxygen is available, and it produces lactate and hydrogen ions as a by-product. Because the blood is not flowing, those products cannot be carried away and accumulate locally, lowering intramuscular pH, interfering with the calcium handling that permits contraction, and stimulating the small nerve fibres that generate the burning sensation and the growing conscious sense of effort. Muscle glycogen is consumed at a far higher rate than it would be aerobically. The climber slows, then stops, and only then does flow resume. Relaxation reverses all of this within seconds. When the muscle goes slack, intramuscular pressure collapses, the vessels reopen, and there is in fact a surge of flow above baseline — reactive hyperaemia — driven by the vasodilating metabolites that accumulated during the squeeze. Simultaneously the relaxation permits the venous muscle pump to refill: leg veins that were compressed flat by the contraction expand and draw blood in, so the next contraction has something to eject. Even a pause of half a second delivers a meaningful pulse of perfusion, and one to two seconds delivers a great deal. The rest step exploits this by ensuring that no muscle group is ever under load continuously. Instead of one long ischaemic contraction lasting the whole climb, the climber performs thousands of short contractions each followed by a genuine perfusion window. The total work done is identical; the metabolic conditions under which it is done are entirely different. The same principle appears elsewhere. Cardiac muscle relies on it absolutely: the coronary arteries are squeezed shut during systole and perfuse the heart wall almost entirely during the relaxed diastolic interval, which is why a very fast heart rate, by shortening diastole, can starve the myocardium. And it is why holding a heavy suitcase still is far more unpleasant than carrying the same suitcase while swapping hands. In every case the variable that matters is not how much force is produced but whether the muscle is ever allowed to let go.

sections.heading: Skeletal Lock: Standing on Bone Rather Than Muscle
sections.body: The second half of the mechanism is mechanical rather than metabolic, and it is the part beginners most often fail to perform. When the knee is bent, the line of body weight passing down through the hip falls behind the knee joint, creating a flexion moment that the quadriceps must actively resist. The deeper the bend, the larger that moment; at a 60 degree knee bend the quadriceps force required can be several times body weight. Hold that position and you are performing a sustained isometric contraction, precisely the condition that occludes perfusion. When the knee is straightened, the weight-bearing line moves forward to pass at or in front of the joint centre, and the posterior ligaments and the bony geometry of the joint take the load. The femur and tibia stack in a nearly straight column and body weight passes down through bone into the ground. The quadriceps can go completely slack. This is the same trick a horse uses to sleep standing up and the same one a fatigued soldier uses at attention, and in the knee it is helped by the so-called screw-home mechanism: in the last 20 or 30 degrees of extension the tibia rotates externally about 5 to 10 degrees relative to the femur, tightening the cruciate and collateral ligaments and locking the joint into its most stable, most congruent, close-packed position. The hip must be extended too, so that the trunk is stacked over the leg rather than leaning forward, or the hip extensors and lower back will simply take over the work the quadriceps just put down. Practised properly, the climber in the pause phase is a balanced tower of bone, and the only muscles doing meaningful work are the small ankle stabilisers and the postural muscles of the trunk. A caution is warranted here, because instructions to lock the knee are sometimes given too bluntly. A brief passive lock at the end of range is normal, safe and is what the joint evolved to do. Slamming into hyperextension repeatedly, particularly for people with hypermobile joints, genu recurvatum, or a history of anterior or posterior cruciate injury, is not advisable. Those climbers should use a soft lock, extending to perhaps five degrees short of full straight, which captures most of the muscular relief while keeping the ligaments off their end-stop. Anyone who feels a sharp or clicking sensation at full extension should stop locking and get the knee assessed. Notice how much of the body participates in this stack. The ankle must sit flat, which is why the technique degrades on very steep ground; the knee provides the lock; the hip must extend so the pelvis sits over the foot; and the trunk must be upright, because a forward lean of even fifteen degrees puts the centre of mass ahead of the support and forces the posterior chain to hold you up. A useful image is a column of coins, each joint stacked over the one below with the load passing straight down the middle. The moment any one joint drifts out of line, the muscles crossing it are back at work.

sections.heading: The Movement Broken Down
sections.body: Described in full, one rest step cycle has four distinct phases, and the whole skill lies in keeping them distinct rather than blurring them into ordinary walking. Phase one is the placement: the unweighted upper foot is lifted and set down on a chosen spot higher up the slope, with no weight yet transferred onto it. Phase two is the drive: weight shifts forward and up onto the new foot, and the leg extends to lift the body. Phase three is the lock: as that leg reaches full extension the climber deliberately straightens it completely, stacks the hip over it, and stands. Phase four is the pause and swing: while standing locked, the climber relaxes the trailing leg entirely and lets it hang and swing forward loosely under gravity, taking one or more breaths before beginning the next placement. The subjective sensation that tells you it is working is very specific and worth hunting for: a distinct feeling of the thigh going soft and heavy for a moment, sometimes accompanied by a faint warm flush as blood returns. If you cannot feel that, you are not fully unloading. Two details separate a good rest step from a poor one. First, the pause happens at the top of the step, standing on the higher leg, not at the bottom. Pausing with the weight on the lower leg simply prolongs the bent-knee isometric hold you are trying to escape. Second, the trailing leg must be genuinely limp during the pause. Many climbers keep it lightly loaded as a sort of outrigger for balance, which defeats the purpose for that leg. Balance instead over the locked leg, and if that feels precarious, widen the stance slightly or use a pole.
steps: Stand on a slope with your weight fully on the lower leg, knee straight and locked, hip stacked directly over the foot so your skeleton carries you.
Consciously relax the upper leg completely. Let it dangle so that the foot rests on the ground with no load through it. Feel the thigh go slack.
Take one full breath in this position. At low altitude this may be a single quick breath; higher up, take two or three, exhaling forcefully through pursed lips.

Place the upper foot on your chosen spot: a flat step, a solid rock, a compacted patch of snow. Keep the step short — aim to gain 15 to 25 centimetres of height, not the biggest stride you can manage.
Transfer weight smoothly onto the upper foot and extend that leg to lift your body, using a steady push rather than a lunge or bounce.
As you arrive, straighten that leg fully and lock the knee, bringing your hips over the foot so you are standing tall rather than leaning into the hill.
Immediately relax the now-trailing lower leg. Let it hang. This is the rest; hold it for the count of one breath or more.
Swing the relaxed trailing leg forward loosely, without lifting it with the hip flexors any more than necessary, and place it for the next step. Repeat, alternating sides so both legs get the pause.

sections.heading: Breathing: Rhythm and Pressure Breathing
sections.body: Breathing is not a separate topic bolted onto the rest step; it is the metronome that drives it. The standard practice is to couple breath to step in a fixed ratio and then change the ratio rather than the technique as the ground steepens or the air thins. Near sea level on moderate ground a fit climber may take one breath per step, or even one breath per two steps. Above about 4,000 metres a common pattern is one full breath per step. Above 7,000 metres two or three breaths per step is normal, and near the summits of the highest peaks climbers have described taking eight, ten or more breaths for a single pace. The ratio itself is unimportant; what matters is that it is fixed and conscious, because a fixed ratio makes the pace self-regulating. If you cannot maintain the ratio, you are going too fast and must shorten the step, not breathe faster. That single rule prevents most of the ragged, stop-start collapse that ruins long ascents. Pressure breathing is the specific altitude adaptation of this rhythm, popularised in the English-speaking climbing world by American guides and Himalayan climbers including Ed Viesturs, though the technique is older than any individual advocate. The climber inhales normally, then exhales forcefully against partly closed or pursed lips, so that the breath comes out with an audible hiss and the cheeks puff slightly. The rationale has two parts. Forcing the exhalation increases the volume actually moved and empties the lungs more completely, so the next inhalation draws in a larger share of fresh air rather than re-breathing stale gas from the airways. Exhaling against resistance raises pressure within the airways and alveoli, which helps hold small airways and alveoli open at the end of expiration, improves the match between ventilation and blood flow in the lung, and may slightly raise the alveolar oxygen pressure available for transfer. It functions rather like the pursed-lip breathing taught to people with chronic lung disease. It is worth being honest that the controlled physiological evidence for pressure breathing at altitude is thinner than its popularity suggests; much of the support is experiential rather than experimental. What is well established is that deliberate, deep, forceful breathing counteracts the shallow, rapid, inefficient panting that hypoxia and anxiety produce, and that alone justifies the practice. Never hold your breath during the effort phase of a step, which raises chest pressure and impedes venous return. A physiological detail explains why depth beats rate. Each breath must first refill the conducting airways, the trachea and bronchi where no gas exchange occurs, which hold roughly 150 millilitres in an adult. Breathe 500 millilitres twelve times a minute and 4.2 litres per minute reaches the alveoli; breathe 250 millilitres twenty-four times a minute, the same total ventilation, and only 2.4 litres reaches them. Rapid shallow panting is therefore close to the worst possible breathing pattern, and it is precisely the pattern a frightened, oxygen-starved climber falls into. The conscious slow deep rhythm of the rest step is the antidote, and it also has a marked calming effect.

sections.heading: Cadence, Pace and Finding a Sustainable Effort
sections.body: The most common reason a climber has to stop is not that the technique failed but that the pace was wrong from the first hundred metres. The rest step is a pacing device as much as a movement pattern, and it works by making the pause the fixed element and the step length the variable. On easy ground you take a longer step and a short pause; as the slope steepens or the altitude bites you shorten the step towards a few centimetres and lengthen the pause. The rhythm never breaks. Novices reverse this, keeping a comfortable stride and simply moving slower and more erratically until they have to halt. The physiological target is to stay at or just below the first ventilatory threshold, the intensity at which lactate first begins to accumulate faster than it can be cleared. In practice this is the conversational pace: you can speak a full sentence, not just three words, without gasping. It corresponds for most people to roughly 60 to 75 percent of maximum heart rate, though the talk test is the more reliable field measure. Above that threshold your carbohydrate stores are consumed disproportionately fast and fatigue becomes cumulative rather than recoverable. Below it, a fit person can keep going for many hours. For planning, Naismith's rule remains the durable starting point: proposed by the Scottish mountaineer William W. Naismith in 1892, it allows one hour for every 5 kilometres of horizontal distance plus one additional hour for every 600 metres of ascent. It assumes a fit party on reasonable ground with a light load and no stops, so most real parties should add a correction. Tranter's corrections adjust for fitness and fatigue, and a rough working practice is to add 25 to 50 percent for a heavy pack, poor conditions or a large group. A useful independent yardstick is vertical rate: 300 metres of ascent per hour is a solid pace for a fit party carrying a pack; 500 to 600 metres per hour is strong; 150 metres per hour is normal above 7,000 metres and is not a sign of weakness. Finally, respect the difference between a rest step and a rest. The rest step postpones the need for halts, but on any climb longer than an hour you still need proper stops of five to ten minutes to eat, drink, adjust clothing and check the weather. There is also a strong argument for starting deliberately slower than feels natural for the first twenty to thirty minutes. Oxygen uptake takes several minutes to rise to meet a new workload, and during that lag any deficit is covered anaerobically; charging off at the trailhead therefore builds a metabolic debt before you have even warmed up, and that debt is paid back with interest for the rest of the day. Experienced parties are recognisable by how slowly they leave the car park. A final measure is to count: on a long, dull, steep section, counting steps in blocks of fifty or a hundred gives an external rhythm and a concrete unit of progress when the summit is still hours away.

sections.heading: Origins and the Mountaineering Tradition
sections.body: The rest step has no single inventor, and claims that it was devised by any particular guide or expedition should be treated sceptically. It appears to have emerged independently wherever people have had to move loads uphill for long periods, and versions of it are described in the walking practices of Sherpa and Balti porters, Andean campesinos, Alpine guides and Himalayan pilgrims long before anyone wrote it down as a technique. What the twentieth-century mountaineering literature did was name it, analyse it and teach it systematically. The canonical written treatment in English is in Mountaineering: The Freedom of the Hills, first published by The Mountaineers of Seattle in 1960 and revised through many editions since; it is that book more than any other that made the rest step a standard item in climbing instruction across the English-speaking world. Alpine guiding traditions in Chamonix and Zermatt taught essentially the same thing under different names, often simply as the guide's pace or, in French climbing usage, as a matter of finding le rythme. Accounts from the great Himalayan expeditions of the 1950s onwards are full of it, often described as the only way movement remained possible above 7,500 metres. Climbers on Everest and K2 have repeatedly reported the pattern of a step, then a long lean on the axe, then many breaths, then another step, gaining perhaps a hundred metres of height in an hour. The observation shared across all these traditions is that practised mountain people walk uphill markedly more slowly than fit visitors at the start of a day and arrive markedly sooner, because they never stop. This is worth taking seriously as a piece of transmitted knowledge, not just as folklore. A porter carrying 30 kilograms who has walked mountain trails since childhood has, in effect, run a lifelong experiment in energy economy, and the pattern that emerges — short strides, locked support leg, continuous unhurried rhythm, few halts, controlled breathing — is the rest step whether it is called that or not. Two related traditional techniques belong beside it. The tortoise-and-hare principle of never exceeding a pace you could hold all day is its strategic counterpart. And the practice of a fixed load-carrying rhythm, sometimes reinforced by counting, chanting or a song, is the same discipline applied through a different channel. What all of them share is the recognition that in the mountains the currency is not speed but the ability to keep producing effort hour after hour without accumulating a debt you cannot repay. There is a corollary that instructors repeat because it is repeatedly ignored. The rest step is a low-status technique. It looks slow, it looks unathletic, and a strong newcomer surrounded by peers will feel foolish adopting it while others stride away. That social pressure is the single largest obstacle to learning it, and it resolves itself around the third hour, when the striders are sitting on rocks and the plodder walks past. Guides in every mountain range have a version of the same observation: the party that arrives first is almost never the party that started fastest.

sections.heading: Snow, Scree and Talus: Terrain Variants
sections.body: The rest step is a rhythm, not a fixed footfall, and it adapts to the surface underneath. On firm snow the technique is at its best, because you can place a foot exactly where you want it and it stays. On soft snow the essential adaptation is to kick or stamp a positive platform before committing weight, and to accept that the pause now serves a second purpose: it gives the snow a moment to consolidate under the foot before you load it. On a moderate snow slope, the duck-walk — feet splayed outward, toes pointing away from each other, sometimes called the duck foot or pied en canard — lets you keep the ankle comfortable and the boot sole flat on the snow well past the angle at which walking straight up becomes awkward, and it pairs naturally with the rest step because the splayed stance is stable enough to balance on one locked leg. Steeper still and you abandon it for kick-stepping straight up or for diagonal ascent on a rising traverse. On scree, the small loose stone that slides underfoot, the difficulty is that the platform moves. The answer is a short step onto the flat of the foot, a moment of stillness to let the surface settle, and only then the weight transfer — which is precisely the rest step's natural pattern, so scree is one of the places where the technique pays off most obviously. Avoid the instinct to lunge, which drives the scree downhill and wastes the energy. On talus, the larger blocky rock of boulder fields, the technique changes character. Here the enemy is not muscular fatigue but the balance and concentration cost of choosing each placement, and blocks may rock or shift when loaded. Test a doubtful block with partial weight before committing, keep steps small enough that you can reverse them, and prefer stepping on the middle of a block rather than an edge. The pause is still valuable but is shorter, because on rough ground the legs get intermittent relief anyway from the varying step heights. On a grassy or muddy trail the risk is simply slipping backward during the drive phase; shorten the step and place the foot flat rather than on the toe. Across all these surfaces, one rule holds: choose the flattest, most solid placement within easy reach rather than the highest one available. Two further conditions deserve mention. On a well-made staircase of steps cut in rock or built as a path, the temptation is to take them at their own rhythm, which is often too tall for efficiency; where the steps are high, use the corner or the side, or take two shorter movements on one riser. And in deep unconsolidated snow, where every step sinks to the knee or thigh, the effort of breaking trail can be two or three times that of following it. Here the correct group technique is to rotate the leader every few minutes rather than letting the strongest member break trail until exhausted, and each follower should step precisely in the leader's footprints.

sections.heading: Steep Ground, Traverses and Zigzags
sections.body: As the angle increases, the geometry of walking straight up becomes untenable long before the ground becomes technically difficult. The limit is set by the ankle. To keep the sole flat on the slope while walking directly uphill, the ankle must dorsiflex through an angle equal to the slope angle plus whatever the step itself demands, and most people run out of dorsiflexion somewhere around 20 to 30 degrees, sooner in stiff mountaineering boots. Beyond that the heel lifts, the weight goes onto the ball of the foot, the calf must work continuously to hold it, and the rest step's locked-leg pause becomes impossible because you can no longer stand flat-footed. There are three standard responses. The first is the diagonal ascent, taking a line at an angle across the fall line rather than straight up. This reduces the effective gradient underfoot, restores a flat-footed stance and allows the rest step to continue unchanged, at the cost of extra distance. On a traverse the uphill leg does more of the lifting, so alternate the direction periodically to share the load; the classic pattern is a series of long zigzags with a change of direction at each end. Learn to make the turn cleanly, stepping through with the uphill foot and pivoting so you never end up crossing your feet awkwardly on steep ground. The second response is the duck-walk described for snow, splaying the feet to buy another five or ten degrees of usable angle. The third, on genuinely steep snow or ice, is to abandon flat-footing altogether and kick straight in with the toes, or front-point on crampons, at which point the calf is under sustained load and the rest step gives way to a different economy: short bursts with deliberate full stops to drop the heels and let the calves drain. On mixed ground it is worth consciously naming to yourself which mode you are in, because the commonest error is drifting into front-pointing on ground that could still be flat-footed, which burns calf endurance you will need later. Crampon technique has its own vocabulary for this: pied à plat or French technique keeps all points flat on the ice and preserves the flat-footed economy far up steep slopes, while pied assis and front-pointing trade economy for security and speed on the steepest ground. Two geometric points are worth carrying in your head when choosing a line. First, a diagonal at 45 degrees to the fall line roughly halves the gradient underfoot but multiplies the distance walked by about 1.4, so the trade is usually favourable but not free. Second, on any slope where a slip would run out badly, the flat-footed diagonal is not merely more comfortable but more secure, because the whole boot sole or every crampon point is engaged rather than two front points. The commonest serious mistake on moderate snow is a tired climber quietly switching to a toe-in shuffle without noticing, which reduces both purchase and endurance at exactly the moment when both matter most. Check yourself for it periodically by asking whether your heels are still touching.

sections.heading: Trekking Poles and the Ice Axe
sections.body: The upper body can take a real share of the work, and on a long ascent that share matters. Trekking poles used correctly transfer somewhere in the region of 5 to 20 percent of the load off the legs onto the arms and shoulders, with published estimates varying widely because the answer depends heavily on gradient, technique and how hard the user actually pushes. What is more consistently demonstrated is that poles reduce peak forces at the knee, improve balance on uneven ground, and lower the perceived exertion of an ascent even where the measured oxygen cost is unchanged or slightly higher, because the work is spread across more muscle. For the rest step specifically, poles matter most because they make the one-legged locked stance easy to balance, so you can genuinely relax the trailing leg instead of leaving it half-loaded as an outrigger. Set the poles shorter than for flat walking — as a rule of thumb about 5 to 10 centimetres shorter for a steep ascent, so that the elbow sits near 90 degrees with the tip planted uphill of you. Plant them in rhythm with the step, typically the opposite pole to the leading leg, and push down as you drive up rather than merely leaning on them. Use the straps correctly, bringing the hand up through the loop and gripping over it, so weight goes through the strap and the wrist rather than through a tight grip, which fatigues the forearm. On any ground where a slip could turn into a slide, however, the ice axe replaces the poles and the priorities change. Carried in the self-arrest or cane position, the axe is held by the head with the pick pointing backward, the shaft driven into the snow uphill of you at each step, and the uphill hand always on it. This is a self-belay, not a walking aid: each plant is an anchor you could hold onto if a foot slipped. Swap hands at every change of direction so the axe is always on the uphill side, which is the one detail beginners most often forget on a zigzag. Some climbers use one pole and one axe on moderate ground, a reasonable compromise. Learn self-arrest properly on a safe practice slope with a runout before relying on any of it; carrying an axe you cannot use is worse than useless because it invites commitment to ground you cannot protect. There is a real cost to poles as well as a benefit, and it should be weighed. Poles occupy both hands, a liability the moment you need to scramble, catch yourself, or deploy an axe in a hurry. There is also evidence that the total energy cost of poled walking is slightly higher than unpoled at the same speed, because the arms are doing work. The sensible reading is that poles trade a small increase in whole-body energy expenditure for a meaningful reduction in leg-specific fatigue and joint loading — on a long day with a heavy pack a trade almost always worth making, and on a short scramble not.

sections.heading: Rope Teams and Moving as a Group
sections.body: As soon as you are roped together on a glacier, the rest step stops being a personal rhythm and becomes a group one, and this is where many otherwise competent parties come apart. On a glacier rope team the standard spacing between climbers is roughly 10 to 15 metres for a party of three, more for a party of two, chosen so that if one climber breaks through a snow bridge the others are far enough back to be on sound snow and can arrest. The rope between climbers should be kept just off the snow: not taut enough to tug at the person ahead, and never slack enough to loop and drag, because slack is what turns a short drop into a long one and a manageable arrest into an impossible one. Maintaining that condition requires every member to move at the same rate, which in turn requires the whole team to adopt the same step-and-pause rhythm. The convention is that the pace is set by the slowest member and everyone else conforms, not the reverse. In practice, put a moderate, steady climber in front to set the pace, and if there is a strong difference in fitness, load the strongest climber's pack more heavily rather than letting them charge ahead. A leader who repeatedly opens a gap and then waits is doing the worst possible thing: they get no rest while stopped and cold, and the followers get no rhythm at all and are forced into a series of surges. The rest step's fixed cadence makes group pacing far easier because it gives everyone the same audible and visible metronome; teams often synchronise unconsciously within a few minutes. Communication conventions help. Agree a call for slowing down and one for stopping, and agree that anyone may use them without argument. Take rest halts on the schedule, not on demand, so nobody has to admit weakness to get a break; a common arrangement is a short stop every 45 to 60 minutes. On a rope team, stop where the whole team can stand safely, not just where the leader happens to be. And bear in mind that a party moves at the pace of its slowest member whether or not it plans to, so realistic time estimates must be built on that person's rate, not the average. Group size compounds this. Every additional person adds friction: another pack to adjust, another bootlace, another call of nature, another opinion at a junction. A party of two moves at close to individual pace; a party of eight commonly loses 20 to 30 percent of its moving time to regrouping unless it is actively managed. The managements that work are simple and worth agreeing before setting off: designate a leader who sets pace and a sweep who stays behind the last person, agree that nobody passes the leader or falls behind the sweep, and stop the whole group together rather than in a trickle so that everyone gets the same length of rest.

sections.heading: Altitude: Where the Rest Step Earns Its Keep
sections.body: The rest step is useful at any elevation but becomes indispensable with altitude, because altitude attacks precisely the resource the technique conserves. Atmospheric pressure falls roughly exponentially with height: about 100 kilopascals at sea level, near 70 at 3,000 metres, around 54 at 5,000 metres and only about 33 to 34 at the summit of Everest at 8,849 metres. The fraction of oxygen in air stays at 20.9 percent everywhere, so what falls is the partial pressure driving oxygen across the alveolar membrane into blood. At 5,500 metres, roughly half of sea-level pressure, the maximum oxygen a person can consume is reduced by something like 30 to 40 percent even after acclimatisation, and on the highest summits it approaches the level required simply to lie still. Under those conditions any anaerobic effort is catastrophically expensive because there is no aerobic reserve to repay the debt, so the disciplined avoidance of ischaemic muscle contraction that the rest step provides stops being a refinement and becomes the only way to move at all. Acclimatisation is what makes altitude survivable, and it works over days: increased ventilation within hours, a shift in blood chemistry as the kidney excretes bicarbonate over two to four days, and rising red cell mass over weeks. The standard conservative guidance above about 3,000 metres is to increase the sleeping altitude by no more than 300 to 500 metres per night, with a rest day every 1,000 metres or every three to four days, and to climb high and sleep low where the terrain allows. Acute mountain sickness presents as headache with nausea, poor appetite, fatigue and disturbed sleep, and is common above 2,500 metres. The two dangerous progressions are high-altitude cerebral oedema, signalled by unsteadiness on the feet, confusion or altered behaviour, and high-altitude pulmonary oedema, signalled by breathlessness at rest, a dry then wet cough and marked drop in exercise tolerance. Both are emergencies and the treatment for both is descent, immediately, by at least 500 to 1,000 metres, regardless of how much the summit cost to reach. No breathing technique or pacing method substitutes for descent. The rest step lets you climb at altitude; it does not let you ignore it. Two further altitude effects bear directly on movement. Appetite is suppressed markedly above roughly 5,000 metres, so climbers routinely under-eat by hundreds or thousands of calories a day and lose weight and muscle over a long expedition; eating becomes a deliberate chore rather than a pleasure, and this is one reason a technique that reduces total energy cost matters more the higher you go. And sleep is fragmented by periodic breathing, the waxing and waning pattern with pauses of ten to thirty seconds that most people develop above about 3,000 metres, so the climber begins each day less recovered than at home. Acetazolamide, taken under medical advice, both speeds acclimatisation and reduces periodic breathing, but it is an aid to a sensible ascent profile rather than a substitute for one.

sections.heading: Fuelling, Hydration and Staying Warm on a Long Ascent
sections.body: Perfect technique cannot outrun an empty tank. Sustained uphill walking with a pack is one of the most energetically expensive things a human body does outside of running, costing on the order of 500 to 900 kilocalories per hour for a moderately fit person on a steep slope with 15 kilograms on their back. The limiting store is muscle and liver glycogen, of which a well-fed adult holds roughly 400 to 600 grams in total, about 1,600 to 2,400 kilocalories. At a conversational aerobic pace a substantial share of energy comes from fat, which stretches that store considerably, but push above the ventilatory threshold and carbohydrate use rises sharply and the store empties in two to three hours. That emptying is what climbers call hitting the wall or bonking: a sudden, disproportionate collapse of pace, clumsiness and low mood. The countermeasure is to eat before you need to, from the first hour, at a rate of roughly 30 to 60 grams of carbohydrate per hour, rising towards 90 grams per hour only if you have trained your gut to tolerate mixed glucose and fructose sources. Small frequent amounts work far better than large occasional ones, because at altitude and under effort the gut tolerates less. Hydration matters comparably and is easier to get wrong at altitude, where the respiratory water loss from breathing very cold, very dry air in large volumes can reach 1 to 2 litres per day on its own, on top of sweat. Thirst is an unreliable guide during exertion and is blunted further by cold and hypoxia, so drink to a schedule: roughly 400 to 800 millilitres per hour in warm conditions, less in cold, and check urine colour at stops. Do not overdrink plain water for many hours while sweating heavily, because dilutional hyponatraemia is a real and occasionally fatal risk on long hot ascents; include some sodium, whether from food, electrolyte tablets or salted snacks. Finally, thermoregulation interacts directly with the rest step, because the technique's long pauses mean you generate less heat per minute than a climber pushing hard. Dress to be slightly cool while moving and add a layer at every stop before you feel cold, not after; the standard discipline is to start a climb feeling underdressed. Wet clothing from over-heating early is the classic route to being cold and miserable at the top. Two practical mechanics make all of this easier to actually do. Keep food and water where you can reach them without taking the pack off, in hip-belt pockets or a shoulder-strap bottle holder, because anything requiring a full stop will be skipped. And in freezing conditions, carry water in insulated bottles stored upside down, since ice forms first at the surface and an inverted bottle therefore freezes at the base rather than sealing the mouth; hydration-bladder hoses freeze notoriously and are a poor choice below about minus five degrees Celsius unless they can be blown clear after every drink. Warm sweet drinks in a vacuum flask solve fuel, fluid and warmth together and are the traditional answer for good reason.

sections.heading: Drilling the Technique Until It Is Automatic
sections.body: The rest step feels artificial for the first few hundred metres and then, quite suddenly, feels like the obvious way to walk uphill. Getting to that point takes deliberate practice, because under fatigue or urgency people revert to whatever movement is habitual, and a technique you have only read about will not survive the third hour of a hard day. Practise it somewhere boring and safe rather than on a serious climb. A staircase in a building is genuinely the best training ground, because the step height is uniform, the surface is predictable and you can concentrate entirely on the feeling of the knee locking and the trailing leg going limp. A steep grassy hillside, a stadium's steps or a treadmill on maximum incline all work. The learning target is not speed; it is the ability to detect, in your own body, the difference between a leg that is merely straight and a leg that is genuinely unloaded. Once you can feel it reliably, add a pack, then add fatigue by practising at the end of a long walk rather than the start, because that is when the technique matters and when it is hardest to hold. Expect the discipline to be the difficulty rather than the movement.
steps: Find a flight of at least twenty steps, or a steep hill with consistent footing. Start with no pack.

Walk up using an exaggerated version: step, lock the knee completely, stand tall, and hold for a full slow count of three before the next step. It will feel absurdly slow. Do the whole flight this way.
Repeat, and this time close your eyes for a few steps at a time where it is safe to do so, so you have nothing to attend to but the sensation of the trailing thigh going slack.
Now add a breath ratio: one full breath during each pause, exhaling forcefully through pursed lips. Keep the ratio absolutely constant for the whole flight.
Shorten the pause to a single breath's length and increase the number of flights, aiming for ten to fifteen minutes of continuous movement without breaking rhythm once.
Add a loaded pack, starting with about 10 kilograms, and repeat. Notice that the step length you can sustain shortens; let it, and keep the pause identical.

Practise the transition drill: walk normally for thirty seconds, then switch into rest step without breaking stride, then back. Being able to change gears deliberately is what you actually need in the mountains.
Finally, practise it tired. Do a long walk or run first, then do twenty minutes of rest-step stairs. If the technique survives that, it will survive a mountain.

sections.heading: Common Errors and How to Correct Them
sections.body: Almost every failure of the rest step reduces to one of eight recurring faults, and each has a specific correction. The first and by far the commonest is never actually locking the knee. The climber adopts the slow cadence but keeps a permanent slight bend, which means the quadriceps never releases and the whole benefit is lost while the cost in speed is paid in full. The correction is to exaggerate deliberately: consciously push the knee back to full extension on each step for a hundred steps until the sensation registers. The second is pausing on the wrong leg, resting at the bottom of the step with weight on the bent lower leg rather than at the top on the straight upper one. The third is over-striding. A long step onto a high foothold demands a deep knee bend and a large single effort, which is anaerobic and disproportionately expensive; two short steps almost always cost less than one tall one, so on steep ground look for the intermediate placement rather than the obvious high one. The fourth is leaning into the hill, planting hands on the thighs or hunching forward over the pack. This puts the centre of mass in front of the supporting foot, which makes the skeletal lock impossible and loads the lower back and hip extensors continuously. Stand upright with the hips stacked over the foot, even though the instinct on steep ground is to crouch. The fifth is holding the breath during the drive phase, which raises intrathoracic pressure, impedes venous return and produces light-headedness; the fix is the fixed breath ratio. The sixth is keeping the trailing leg lightly weighted for balance, which halves the benefit. The seventh is a variable rhythm, speeding up on easier sections and grinding to a halt on steeper ones, which is exactly backwards; the rhythm should be constant and the step length should absorb the change in gradient. The eighth, and the most insidious on long days, is letting the pause grow so long that you are effectively stopping without admitting it, which chills you, breaks the rhythm and wastes daylight. If your pause has crept past three or four breaths at moderate altitude, the honest reading is that you are over-paced or under-fuelled, and the correct response is a proper stop with food and drink rather than a slow disintegration on your feet. A ninth fault is worth adding because it is invisible to the person committing it: rhythm decay under fatigue. Everyone's technique degrades as the day goes on, and the degradation is gradual enough to escape notice. The remedy is a periodic audit. Every twenty minutes or so, run a deliberate three-point check — is the knee actually locking, is the trailing leg actually limp, is the breath ratio actually fixed — and correct whatever has slipped. Climbers who do this reliably report that at least one of the three has drifted almost every time, which is the strongest argument for making it a habit rather than trusting the technique to hold itself together.

sections.heading: Descent, Limits and Knowing When to Turn Around
sections.body: The rest step is an ascent technique and does not transfer to going down, which is a different physiological problem entirely. Descending loads the quadriceps eccentrically, meaning the muscle lengthens while contracting to control the fall, and eccentric contractions generate high force at low metabolic cost while producing far more microscopic muscle damage. That is why a long descent leaves you barely out of breath and yet crippled with delayed-onset muscle soreness two days later, and why the majority of mountain injuries and a large share of fatal slips occur on the way down, when climbers are tired, satisfied and hurrying. The descent techniques are their own subject — short steps, a slightly bent knee absorbing the shock rather than a straight one, poles lengthened, plunge-stepping in soft snow with the heel driven in and weight committed confidently — and the governing principle is to plan the descent as a full leg of the journey with its own time budget. It is also worth stating plainly what the rest step cannot do. It does not increase your maximum aerobic capacity, so it will not make you faster on a short climb where speed is the limit. It does not help on technical rock or steep ice where hand-and-foot movement governs. It does not offset inadequate acclimatisation, dehydration, an empty stomach, or a plan that was too ambitious to begin with. Above all, it does not manage risk. Turning around is a skill in its own right, and the discipline that makes it possible is setting a hard turnaround time before you leave, in daylight and good humour, and honouring it regardless of how close the summit looks. A workable rule for a long day is to fix the turnaround so that you reach easy ground before dark with an hour in hand, and to treat the halfway point of your available time as the latest moment for reaching the summit. Turn around early and without debate if any of the following appear: worsening headache unrelieved by rest and fluid, vomiting, stumbling or unsteady walking, breathlessness while standing still, a wet cough, a member of the party who has stopped eating or talking, deteriorating visibility or a rising wind, or simply the arithmetic showing you will not make it. The mountain is a fixed object and will be there next season. The most reliable predictor of a long climbing life is not strength or technique but a consistent willingness to go home. The psychological trap has a name in the mountaineering literature: summit fever, the progressive discounting of risk as the objective comes within reach, reinforced by everything already invested in getting there. It is a textbook case of the sunk-cost fallacy operating in a place where the penalty for it is death. The countermeasures are structural rather than motivational, because willpower is exactly the faculty that fails when hypoxic and tired: fix the turnaround time in writing before departure, give every member an unopposed veto, and agree in advance the signs that end the day. Decide it in the valley; let the person on the mountain merely execute.

guides.safetyNote: Efficient movement does not make dangerous ground safe. Steep snow, glaciers, rockfall and altitude kill regardless of technique. Learn crampon, ice axe and rope skills from a qualified instructor before relying on them, ascend slowly enough to acclimatise, and treat worsening headache, vomiting, stumbling or breathlessness at rest as a signal to descend immediately.

sections.heading: River crossings
sections.body:
Moving water is the most underestimated hazard in wilderness travel, because the force it applies rises with the square of its speed. Doubling the current from one metre per second to two quadruples the push against your legs. A knee-deep flow at walking pace is a nuisance; the same depth moving at four or five metres per second, which is a brisk jog and looks unremarkable from the bank, generates enough drag to sweep an adult off their feet. The practical threshold most guiding services use is that depth in metres multiplied by speed in metres per second should stay below about one; above that, competent people are being knocked down. Cold compounds it — in water near freezing, useful hand and leg function is measurably degraded within a few minutes.

Site selection does more for you than technique. Walk the bank and spend real time choosing: an hour spent finding a good crossing is cheaper than any rescue. Look for the widest stretch, because a river spread wide is necessarily shallower and slower than the same volume squeezed into a narrow channel. Prefer a straight reach over a bend, since the outside of a bend is always the deepest and fastest part. Look downstream before anything else and ask what happens if you are swept away: a gravel bar or a slow pool is a survivable outcome, whereas a strainer — a fallen tree or brush pile that water passes through but a body cannot — a waterfall, or a rapid is a reason to reject the site entirely regardless of how good the entry looks. Never cross above any of those.

Prepare before you enter. Undo the hip belt and sternum strap so the pack can be shed instantly; a buckled pack becomes an anchor holding your face under. Keep boots on for grip and to protect your feet, removing socks and inner soles if you want them dry, or carry lightweight crossing shoes. Loosen or remove anything that can catch water like a sail. Move sleeping bag, insulating layers and electronics into a dry bag high in the pack.

The crossing itself is deliberate rather than quick. Face upstream at a slight angle, lean into the current, and shuffle sideways without crossing your feet. Use a stout pole or stick planted upstream as a third point of contact, moving only one of the three at a time. If the water reaches mid-thigh, or you feel gravel moving under your boots, or you cannot see your feet through the flow, retreat while retreat is still cheap. Two or three people linking arms in a line, or gripping a shared pole, is markedly more stable than one. If you do go in, roll onto your back with feet downstream and toes at the surface to fend off rocks, and swim aggressively for the bank at an angle rather than fighting straight across.

sections.heading: Slopes & scree
sections.body:
Descent, not ascent, is where most slope injuries happen. Going uphill your muscles shorten under load, which is tiring but stable; going downhill they lengthen under load — an eccentric contraction — which generates far higher forces, causes most of the delayed muscle soreness people blame on the climb, and degrades control precisely when a slip is most consequential. Peak force through the knee on a steep descent can reach several times body weight per step, and it arrives suddenly. The countermeasure is to shorten the drop per step and increase the number of steps: small steps, high cadence, knees softly bent to act as shock absorbers rather than locked straight.

Body position is counter-intuitive and gets people hurt. The instinct on a steep descent is to lean back into the hill, which feels safer and is not: leaning back shifts your centre of mass behind your feet, reducing the downward force pressing your soles into the ground and letting them skate out from under you. Keep your torso upright or slightly forward so your weight stacks directly over your boots, and let the friction of the sole do its job. Switchback rather than plunging straight down the fall line; traversing at an angle reduces the effective grade, spares the knees, and gives you a route that can be reversed. Trekking poles lengthened by five to ten centimetres for the descent genuinely reduce knee loading and give two extra contact points.

Scree and talus need different techniques from each other and it is worth knowing which you are on. Scree is small, loose, mobile rock, typically finer than a fist. On descent it can be ridden — the scree run, where you plant the heel first and let the surface slide a short distance with each step, keeping weight centred and never letting the slide get faster than a controlled walk. Talus is coarse blocky rock, often from boulder to car-sized, and must never be ridden. Cross it by stepping onto the flat centre of each block rather than the edges, testing before committing weight, and watching for the rocking block that pivots and traps an ankle.

Two hazards deserve naming. Rockfall on loose ground is generated by the party itself, so never climb or descend directly above or below another person; spread out abreast or stagger so nobody is in another's fall line, and shout a warning immediately if you dislodge anything. And the most dangerous slope is often the innocuous-looking one: a moderate grass or gravel slope steep enough to slide on but not steep enough to look threatening, ending in a drop. Judge a slope by where a slide would finish, not by how hard the walking feels.

sections.heading: Ice & snow
sections.body:
Snow and ice change hour by hour with temperature, sun and wind, so the same slope can be safe at dawn and lethal at midday. Firm overnight snow that takes a boot edge cleanly becomes wet, unsupportive slush a few hours after the sun reaches it, and refreezes overnight into hard ice that a boot cannot bite at all. This is why alpine parties start before dawn: the goal is to be off the snow slopes before they soften. Read the surface constantly rather than deciding once.

On firm snow, kicking steps is the fundamental technique. Swing the boot from the knee and let the toe or the edge chop a small ledge, rather than pressing the foot in — momentum does the cutting. Going straight up, kick the toe in and step up onto the platform; traversing, use the side edge of the boot and cut a level shelf wide enough for the whole foot. Descending firm snow, the plunge step drives the heel down hard with a straight-ish leg and the weight fully committed over it; timidity here is what causes slips, because a half-hearted heel skates. If a slope is steep enough that a slip would accelerate and the runout ends in rocks, trees or a drop, you need an ice axe and a practised self-arrest, or you need a different route — crampons and an axe are not optional equipment on hard snow above serious consequences, and self-arrest is a skill that only works if it has been rehearsed to reflex on a safe slope.

Snow bridges over creeks and crevasses, and shelf ice at the edge of a river, are the specific traps that catch travellers who are otherwise doing everything right, because they look continuous with solid ground. Probe ahead with a pole before every committed step where running water might be beneath; a hollow sound, a soft plunge, or visible sag are all reasons to back off. Bridges are strongest in the cold of early morning and weakest in the afternoon. Cross one at right angles, quickly, with the party spread well apart so only one person's weight is ever on it.

Avalanche terrain is a separate discipline and deserves honest treatment rather than a rule of thumb. The great majority of avalanche fatalities occur on slopes between about 30 and 45 degrees, and the victim or their party almost always triggers the slide. The highest-risk windows are during and within 24 to 48 hours of heavy snowfall, during rapid warming or rain on snow, and on lee slopes where wind has loaded a slab. Avoid terrain traps — gullies, and any slope with a run-out into trees or over a cliff — because burial depth and trauma both rise sharply there. If you travel in avalanche country regularly, a formal course, a transceiver, probe and shovel, and the habit of reading the daily forecast are the real answer; nothing written here substitutes for that.

sections.heading: Pace yourself
sections.body:
Endurance on rough ground is a pacing problem far more than a fitness problem. The useful discipline is to move at a rate you could sustain for the whole day and hold a conversation at — the so-called conversational pace, which corresponds roughly to staying below the aerobic threshold. Above that line you begin drawing on glycogen faster than you can replace it and accumulating fatigue you will not recover from until you stop. The classic novice error is racing the first hour, which costs more over the following six than it ever gained. On a sustained climb the rest step is the single most valuable technique: after each step forward, straighten the rear leg completely and pause for a beat so that your skeleton, rather than your thigh muscle, carries the load. It looks absurdly slow and it lets people climb for hours without stopping.

For planning, Naismith's rule remains a serviceable baseline: allow one hour per five kilometres of distance, plus an extra hour for every 600 metres of ascent. It systematically underestimates rough terrain, so add substantially for deadfall, boulder fields, deep snow, or a heavy pack, and remember that descent is not free — steep or loose descent can be as slow as the climb. Tranter's corrections adjust the figure for fitness and fatigue late in the day.

Blisters are the most common trip-ending injury and they are almost entirely preventable, because the tissue damage happens well before the blister appears. A blister is caused by repeated shear — the skin surface held by the sock while deeper layers move with the foot — which separates the epidermis and lets fluid fill the gap. Heat and moisture soften skin and dramatically increase that shear, which is why damp feet blister so much faster. The hot spot, a patch of localised warmth or stinging, is the warning that separation is beginning. Stop the moment you feel one, even if it means unlacing on a windy ridge with the group waiting. Two minutes with tape, a blister plaster or a strip of moleskin over clean dry skin reliably prevents a wound that will otherwise alter every step for days.

Deep soft snow imposes its own arithmetic. Postholing — sinking to the knee or thigh with each step — can multiply the energy cost of travel several times over and reduce progress below one kilometre an hour. The answer is rotation: the lead breaks trail for a short, fixed interval, perhaps fifty steps or five minutes, then steps aside and falls to the back of the line while the next person takes over. Everyone behind walks in the compacted track for a fraction of the effort. Short, frequent leads keep the whole party fresher than long heroic ones, and preserve the group's margin for the unexpected.

sections.heading: Reading the Ground Before You Step: Contour Lines as a Travel Forecast
sections.body:
A topographic map tells you what a slope will feel like under your boots before you ever commit to it, if you learn to read contour spacing as a grade forecast. A contour line joins points of equal elevation, and the vertical distance between adjacent lines — the contour interval, printed in the map margin — is fixed across the sheet. So the only variable is horizontal spacing, and that spacing does the division for you: tightly packed lines mean a lot of height in a little distance, a steep climb; widely spaced lines mean a gentle one. Percent grade is rise over run times 100, and the angle in degrees is the arctangent of that ratio.

Work an example. You are studying a 1:24,000 quadrangle with a 40-foot contour interval, eyeing a cross-country shortcut straight up a drainage instead of following the trail's long switchbacks. At 1:24,000, one inch on the page equals 2,000 feet of ground. Along the trail the contour lines sit about one-twentieth of an inch apart, so each represents roughly 100 feet of horizontal ground — a grade of 40 divided by 100, or 40 percent, about 22 degrees. Steep, but walkable. Now look at the drainage: there the lines bunch to about one-fiftieth of an inch, only 40 feet of ground per line, so the grade jumps to 40 over 40 — 100 percent, a 45-degree pitch. That is effectively a cliff band that no amount of determination converts into a hike. The difference is invisible from below on the ground and obvious from above on the map, which is the whole reason for checking before you climb rather than after.

Two shape patterns are worth memorising because they let you tell a rib from a gully at a glance. On a spur — a descending ridge — the contour lines form a V or U pointing away from the high ground, downhill. In a reentrant or draw, the valley a stream cuts, the same shapes point toward the high ground, uphill. Spurs point down, reentrants point up, and the rule holds on every quadrangle you will ever read. Because water collects in reentrants, they are also where you find brush, deadfall, waterfalls and wet rock, while spurs tend to be drier, more open, and better for travel — which is why experienced parties climb ridges and descend them too.

A saddle or col, the low point on a ridge between two summits where contours pinch into an hourglass, is nearly always the easiest and often the only sane way to cross from one drainage into the next. A great deal of route-finding around dangerous terrain amounts to aiming for the nearest saddle rather than the crest above it. One honest limitation: features shorter than the contour interval simply do not appear. A 10-foot rock step, a fence, or a band of cliffs less than the interval high can be entirely absent from a 40-foot-interval map, so a route that looks clean on paper can still be blocked on the ground. Cross-check with imagery or a local description before committing to an untried line.

sections.heading: Ridgelines, Exposure, and the Discipline of Turning Back
sections.body:
Exposure is a different hazard from steepness: it measures the consequence of a slip, not the difficulty of the step.
